E1106.summary: In Atwood's words, the Word that contains the two catholic natures, the changeable and the immutable.
E1106.body: Atwood speaks of “the two catholic natures contained in the mirific Word” [III.2 ¶24]. From the context of her record, these two natures are the changeable and the immutable. The text gives no further definition here.

E1107.summary: In the Alchemists' teaching as reported, the part of nature that the reduction destroys, as distinct from her vehicle.
E1107.body: This is a view reported from the Alchemists. The modal life is what the reduction destroys, as opposed to nature's vehicle. The context suggests it is her superfluous forms, since nature is said to be addressed “where nature may be addressed in order to the rejection of her superfluous forms” [II.1 ¶47]. That equation is an inference, not the text's own statement.

E1108.summary: An unnamed modern adept whom Atwood cites to support her claim that hiding the truth let ignorance spread.
E1108.body: Atwood cites an unnamed modern adept in support of her point that concealment spread ignorance: “this bushel being placed over the light, the darkness of it invited ignorance abroad” [I.1 ¶64]. She endorses the view.

E1109.summary: Unnamed modern interpreters whom Atwood criticizes for explaining the lights of the Mysteries as orreries and astronomy.
E1109.body: Atwood rejects the reading of unnamed modern interpreters (“as some say”) who explain the lights shown in the Mysteries as orreries and astronomy [II.3 ¶49].

E1110.summary: Modern metaphysicians, whom the Appendix contrasts with its own view because they make Time a condition of thought.
E1110.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), modern metaphysicians are set in contrast because they make Time a condition of thought [APP ¶172].

E1111.summary: Modern metaphysics, which Atwood contrasts with her own view because it treats mind as only abstract or inferential.
E1111.body: Atwood sets modern metaphysics against her own position because it treats mind only as abstract or inferential [III.1 ¶2].

E1112.summary: The moderns and empirical chemists, whom Atwood criticizes: their elements and distilled waters are not what the adepts mean.
E1112.body: Atwood criticizes the moderns and empirical chemists. Their elements and distilled waters are not what the adepts mean, “as the empirical chemists formerly imagined” [I.2 ¶39; I.2 ¶43].

E1113.summary: The fire the matter is to be boiled in, named in Hermes' precept and not explained at that point.
E1113.body: Hermes' precept, which Atwood repeats, says: “Put the matter into a moist fire” [I.3 ¶10]. The moist fire is the fire the matter is boiled in. The passage does not explain it: the nature, origin and “artificial excitation” of the philosophic fire are put off until later.

E1114.summary: In the Poemander, what the descending darkness turns into: an unspeakably troubled moist nature that gives off smoke, with Light before it.
E1114.body: Hermes speaks in the Poemander. The descending darkness changes into “a certain moist nature unspeakably troubled, which yielded a smoke, as from fire” [III.3 ¶53]. It is “that moist nature, that appeareth out of the darkness”, and the Light is before it. When the Word joins Nature, pure fire flies upward out of it [III.3 ¶54].

E1115.summary: In Vaughan's warning, natures that rise against the central fire when excess heat provokes them.
E1115.body: Vaughan warns that too much heat provokes the moist natures: “thou hast stirred up the wrath of the moist natures, and they will stand up against the central fire” [III.4 ¶44]. This is a caution about managing the fire.

E1116.summary: Venus's spirit, to which metalline bodies cling so that it may give them life.
E1116.body: In a footnote, Atwood says metalline bodies cling to Venus's moist spirit so that it can give them life: “they gladly adhere to this moist spirit, that it may vivify them” [I.3 n49].

E1117.summary: The simple unity to which the Ternary is reduced, Nature is brought back by rejecting the Binary, and man is reduced in union with God.
E1117.body: Atwood treats the Monad as the simple unity at the end of the reduction. The Ternary is reduced, and Nature is brought back by rejecting the Binary, “to the simplicity of the Monad” [IV.2 ¶18]. She also speaks of “the Monadic simplicity of her Element” [IV.2 ¶20]. In the Chaldaic oracle she cites, the (Paternal) Monad generates Two and rules the Triad: “The Monad is enlarged which generates Two,” [IV.2 ¶22]. Discussing the Kabalah, she cites the union it describes, “the union of man, reduced to the simplicity of the Monad, with God” [IV.3 ¶27]. On this reading, reducing man to the Monad and reducing Nature to it seem to be the same aim. The text sets the two passages side by side but does not state that link.

E1118.summary: The ordered state in which the renewed faculties and every dignified sentiment are brought into accord under Light.
E1118.body: Atwood uses the phrase for the outcome of renewal. The renewed faculties and every dignified sentiment are brought into accord “to testify and maintain the triumphant Monarchy of Light” [IV.4 ¶20].

E1119.summary: The monk who wrote the Rosary (Rosar., Abbrev. Tract. iii and iv), cited for the teaching that Stone and medicine are one.
E1119.body: Atwood cites the monk in his Rosary (Rosar., Abbrev. Tract. iii and iv) in support of the teaching that the Stone and the medicine are one, with nothing added or taken away: “The Stone is one” [I.2 ¶11; I.2 n11]. She endorses it.

E1120.summary: The monks, whom Atwood criticizes for promoting Agrippa's Vanity as if it were a recantation.
E1120.body: Atwood criticizes the monks for promoting Agrippa's Vanity as a recantation [I.1 ¶64].

E1121.summary: The passive luminary of the Philosophic Heaven: in Atwood's account the Passive Intelligence, paired with the Sun, and named by many authorities in veiled forms.
E1121.body:
**Atwood's statements.** In Alchemy “the Moon is singularly honored, for it is the Passive Intelligence” [III.1 ¶40]. With the Sun, it is one of the pair that “sound the depths together”. Citing Plutarch, she writes that “the influence of the Moon, says Plutarch, seems to reflect the works of reason, and to proceed from Wisdom” [III.1 ¶45]. She also reports that Boehme finds Sol and Luna together at the cross.

**Hermes, glossed by Atwood.** “Luna after fifteen days is diminished; and in the third, she is augmented” [I.3 ¶7]. Atwood explains this Luna as “that ethereal light, which is the passive luminary in the Philosophic Heaven” [I.3 n7]. Its waning and waxing match the moon's, and the philosopher names it after the moon by analogy. Elsewhere Hermes says: “My own Luna, also, is my light, exceeding every other light” [I.3 ¶37]. This is the Stone's own light, and it is not explained further.

**Other quoted authorities.**
- *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon*: the Moon is sister and bride of the Sun, born with him in the Lion's Bed, and with him a parent of the King. Luna holds parallel positions in the poem. She is fed to the Lion with Sol and worked alone with the Lion's blood, “Worke Luna by her selfe alone, With the blood of the Greene Lyon:” [III.1 ¶65], for the white ferment, and she feeds a white King. The passage does not assert that Luna and the Moon are identical.
- Eirenaeus: when the soul imprisoned in Saturn is set free, a shining vapour arises, “A Vapour shining, like pearl orient, Which is our Moon and sparkling Firmament” [III.1 ¶69]. Elsewhere he pairs Sol and Lune as what projection produces: “Most perfect Sol and Lune from fire receive” [IV.3 ¶25]. The next line says they will prove both gold and silver pure.
- The author of the New Light: “our lune or silver, not common silver” [I.3 n40], which receives the seed of gold.
- Pierce, the Black Monk, names Lune among the contents of the seed without explaining it: “In the which is alle, Sol, Lune, Life and Light” [III.4 ¶21].

Asserted identities: Moon = Passive Intelligence [III.1 ¶40]. Luna = the ethereal light or passive luminary of the Philosophic Heaven [I.3 n7]. Moon = the shining Vapour and sparkling Firmament (Eirenaeus) [III.1 ¶69]. Lune = silver, not common silver (New Light) [I.3 n40].

E1122.summary: In Vaughan, a middle Nature that is placed equally within two elements in the vital heat-operation.
E1122.body: Vaughan, as quoted, gives the instruction: “take the Moon of the Firmament, which is a middle Nature” [IV.1 ¶41]. In the vital heat-operation it is placed equally within two elements. He asserts its identity with a middle Nature in the same place.

E1123.summary: The author of Centrum Naturae Concentratum, cited for the claim that man is the best subject and can draw the Central Salt of nature.
E1123.body: Atwood cites the Moorish philosopher (Centrum Naturae Concentratum) in support of the claim that man himself is the best subject and can draw the Central Salt of nature. The cited passage speaks of what “contains not so great mysteries and excellences as Man reformed by God into his image” [II.1 ¶9; II.1 n3]. She endorses this.

E1124.summary: Unnamed observers whose testimony Atwood cites: very few people are naturally suited to the research.
E1124.body: Atwood relies on the testimony of more experienced observers that very few people are naturally suited to the research [III.4 ¶2].

forms: the more modern class of adepts
E1125.summary: Later adepts whom Atwood cites for the view that man's life is a fire capable of improvement.
E1125.body: Atwood cites the more modern class of adepts in support of the view that man's life is a fire capable of improvement: “a pure, naked, and unmingled fire of infinite capability” [II.1 ¶17].

E1126.summary: An unnamed experimentalist cited for the sign of the Arcanum: the masculine tincture rising from the black and uniting with the white spirit.
E1126.body: In a footnote, Atwood cites a more modern experimentalist. When the masculine tincture rises from the black and unites with the white spirit, the operator “will then know that he hath the great Arcanum of the world” [I.3 n53].

E1127.summary: An adept who taught King Calid. Atwood cites him often for the teaching that the matter is taken from man himself, and on the operation.
E1127.body:
**Story.** Morienus was the disciple of an adept, Adfar, and later initiated King Calid. Their dialogue is cited as *Morienus Eremita Hierosol. De Transfiguratione Metallorum* [I.1 ¶35; I.1 n38]. Atwood says his biographer's story is too long to extract.

**The matter.** Atwood takes his advice to Calid as pointing to the matter being taken from man: “This matter, O king, is extracted from thee” [II.1 ¶8; II.1 n1] and “The thing, O king, is extracted from thee” [II.1 ¶16; II.1 n15]. She says Sendivogius diverted this hint. Morien also supports her vessel and place doctrine [II.1 ¶8], and he is counted among the authorities who agree about the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

**The operation.** “Our operation, concludes Morien, is nothing else but extracting water from the earth and returning it again” [IV.1 ¶41; IV.1 n36]. This is an alternating extraction and return of moisture that leads to putrefaction. Atwood then glosses it as action and reaction.

**Other uses.** As cited by Eirenaeus, he warned Calid that many philosophers were overcome by the fatigue of this work [IV.1 ¶6; IV.1 n5]. He supports the teaching that the magistery is God's secret of secrets, entrusted to the prophets: “Scire etiam tibi convenit, O bone rex” (ours: It is fitting also for you to know, O good king) [II.4 ¶39; II.4 n27]. Norton's verse names him among masters who wrote obscurely, “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. Atwood uses him mainly as a supporting authority.

E1128.summary: The unnamed writer of Morienus's story, which Atwood mentions but finds too long to extract.
E1128.body: Atwood mentions that Morienus's biographer tells his story, but she judges it too long to extract [I.1 ¶35].

E1129.summary: Putting the matter to death as a necessary step of the work. For Atwood, it is the death of the fiery self-willed agent once it is ripe.
E1129.body: Hermes makes mortification necessary, together with generation: “except one understandeth how to mortify and induce generation” [I.3 ¶26]. That is, the matter must be put to death through its proper nature. Atwood applies the term to the fiery, self-willed agent. It grows to its full extent “until the time for his mortification is ripe and ready at hand” [III.1 ¶56]. The connate spirit then finally brings the agent to this death, so it becomes a self-mortification.

E1130.summary: The Mosaic Scripture. Some learned writers held it to be the only revealed truth; Atwood would still revere it if all cosmogonies share one divine source.
E1130.body: Atwood reports that some learned writers judged that “the Mosaic was the only revealed truth of all” [III.3 ¶42]. She qualifies this view. If all cosmogonies share one divine source, she would still revere Scripture.

E1131.summary: A figure whom Atwood cites as one who taught under a veil and whose legitimate power she sets against the Egyptians' enchantments.
E1131.body: Like Hermes, Moses gives his instruction under a veil [I.3 n40]. In the Apostle's text she quotes, the Law is read under a veil: “when Moses is read, the veil is upon their heart” [III.3 ¶59]. Atwood compares him on the waters: those on which the Spirit of God moved are not common water [I.2 ¶43]. He appears with Ezekiel, David and Zachariah as illustrating the Wheel of Fire, in which all things are transfigured [II.3 ¶54]. Boehme names him with the Prophets, Christ and the Apostles as teaching what Boehme finds in his inner book [III.2 ¶16]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Moses' legitimate power under God's law, “might in word and deed”, is set against the Egyptians' enchantments [APP ¶2; APP ¶4].

E1132.summary: Philosophers whom Atwood cites in support of the difference between common and natural calcination.
E1132.body: Atwood appeals to the most enlightened philosophers in support of the difference between common and natural calcination [IV.3 ¶16].

E1133.summary: The great mystery in which, Atwood says, we stand even now.
E1133.body: Atwood writes: “And so far we stand even now in the great mystery, in the Mother of all beings” [III.3 ¶52]. The passage does not define the term further.

E1134.summary: Something Atwood expects to come forth in the Fourth Monarchy; the text does not define it further.
E1134.body: Atwood looks ahead to a time “when the Mother of sciences will come forth” [IV.3 ¶49], in the Fourth Monarchy. The term is not defined further.

E1135.summary: The operator's motive, which Atwood calls the true spiritual ferment: everything depends on it, and the Work truly begins only when the right Motive is found.
E1135.body: For Atwood, the Motive is decisive: “Everything depends upon the Motive, which is the true spiritual ferment” [IV.1 ¶44]. The result corresponds to the virtue of the Motive, and the Work truly begins only then, since “it is not until the right Motive is discovered” [IV.1 ¶48]. She identifies the Motive with the spiritual ferment [IV.1 ¶44].
